items.new: But since the highest truth lives only in landlessness — shoreless and boundless as God — it is better to perish in that howling infinity than to be ingloriously dashed against the lee shore, even if that shore meant safety! For who would crawl to land like a cowardly worm! Terrors of the terrible! Is all this agony in vain? Take heart, take heart, O Bulkington! Bear up grimly, demigod! Up from the spray of your ocean death — straight up — leaps your apotheosis!

items.new: No dignity in whaling? The very heavens bear witness to the dignity of our calling. Cetus is a constellation in the southern sky! Enough said! Jam your hat down firmly in the presence of the Czar, and take it off to Queequeg! Enough said! I know a man who, in his lifetime, has taken three hundred and fifty whales. I consider that man more honorable than that great captain of antiquity who boasted of taking as many walled towns.

items.new: Starbuck was no crusader after dangers; in him courage was not a sentiment but a thing simply useful to him, and always at hand on every practical occasion where life and death were at stake. Besides, he thought, perhaps, that in this business of whaling, courage was one of the great staple supplies of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted. So he had no liking for lowering the boats for whales after sundown, nor for persisting in fighting a whale that persisted too much in fighting him. For, thought Starbuck, I am here on this critical ocean to kill whales for my living, and not to be killed by them for theirs; and Starbuck knew well that hundreds of men had been killed that way. What fate had been his own father's? Where, in the bottomless depths, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?

items.new: Stubb was the second mate. He was a native of Cape Cod, and so, according to local usage, was called a Cape-Cod-man. A happy-go-lucky type; neither cowardly nor valiant; taking dangers as they came with an indifferent air; and in the most urgent crisis of the chase, toiling away, calm and collected as a journeyman joiner hired for the year. Good-humored, easy, and carefree, he presided over his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were only a dinner, and his crew all invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat as an old stagecoach driver is about the snugness of his seat. When close to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his pitiless lance coolly and offhandedly, as a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while flank to flank with the most furious monster. Long habit had, for this Stubb, turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought of death itself, there is no telling. Whether he ever thought of it at all might be a question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it to be a sort of call of the watch, telling all hands to tumble aloft and get busy there about something he would find out when he obeyed the order, and not sooner.

items.new: Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black negro-savage, with a lion-like tread — an Ahasuerus to behold. Hanging from his ears were two golden hoops, so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts, and would talk of securing the topsail halyards to them. In his youth Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler lying in a lonely bay on his native coast. And having never been anywhere in the world but Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most visited by whalemen, and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners unusually careful about what sort of men they shipped, Daggoo kept all his barbaric virtues, and, erect as a giraffe, moved about the decks in all the pomp of six feet five in his socks. There was a bodily humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg a truce of a fortress. Curious to say, this imperial negro, Ahasuerus Daggoo, was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's company, let it be said that at the present day not one in two of the many thousand men before the mast employed in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. In this the American whale fishery is the same as the American army and the military and merchant navies, and the engineering forces employed in building the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases the native American liberally provides the brains, and the rest of the world as generously supplies the muscles. No small number of these whaling seamen belong to the Azores, where the outward-bound Nantucket whalers often call to fill out their crews from the hardy peasants of those rocky shores. In the same way, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London put in at the Shetland Islands to take on their full complement of crew, and on the passage home they drop them there again. How it is, there is no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders in the Pequod — Isolatoes too, as I call them, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel, what a set these Isolatoes were! An Anacharsis Clootz deputation from all the isles of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab in the Pequod to lay the world's grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back. Black little Pip — he never did — oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle you shall soon see him, beating his tambourine; a prelude to the eternal time when, sent for to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to strike in with the angels and beat his tambourine in glory; called a coward here, hailed a hero there!

items.new: Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft to see if any strange face was visible; for my first vague uneasiness about the unknown captain, now in the seclusion of the sea, had become almost an agitation. This was strangely heightened at times by the ragged Elijah's diabolical, incoherent ramblings, which came back to me uninvited, with a subtle energy I could not have imagined before. I could only poorly withstand them, much as in other moods I was almost ready to smile at the solemn whims of that outlandish prophet of the wharves. But whatever apprehension or uneasiness — to call it that — I felt, whenever I came to look around me in the ship, it seemed against all reason to cherish such feelings. For though the harpooners, with the great body of the crew, were a far more barbaric, heathenish, and motley set than any of the tame merchant-ship companies I had known before, I still put this down — and rightly — to the fierce uniqueness of the very nature of that wild Scandinavian calling in which I had so recklessly embarked. But it was above all the look of the three chief officers of the ship, the mates, that was most strongly fitted to allay these colorless misgivings and to inspire confidence and cheerfulness about every prospect of the voyage. Three better, more promising sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American: a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, a Cape man. Now, since it was Christmas when the ship shot out of her harbor, for a while we had biting polar weather, though all the time we were running away from it to the southward; and with every degree and minute of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter and all its intolerable weather behind us. It was on one of those mornings of the transition, less threatening but still gray and gloomy enough, when with a fair wind the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping and melancholy speed, that I climbed to the deck at the call of the forenoon watch; and the moment I leveled my gaze toward the taffrail at the stern, foreboding shivers ran over me. Reality outran apprehension: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

items.new: Soon after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the now sunny deck, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. The mates were fully capable of handling nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing. So there was little or nothing outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab now, and so to chase away, for that one interval, the clouds that were piled layer upon layer on his brow — just as all clouds always choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.

items.new: "I never had such a queer dream, King-Post. You know the old man's ivory leg? Well, I dreamed he kicked me with it; and when I tried to kick back, upon my soul, my little man, I kicked my leg right off! And then, presto! Ahab seemed to be a pyramid, and I, like a blazing fool, kept kicking at it. But what was still more curious, Flask — you know how curious all dreams are — through all this rage I was in, I somehow seemed to be thinking to myself that, after all, it wasn't much of an insult, that kick from Ahab. 'Why,' thinks I, 'what's the row? It's not a real leg, only a false leg.' And there's a mighty difference between a living thump and a dead thump. That's what makes a blow from the hand, Flask, fifty times more savage to bear than a blow from a cane. The living limb — that's what makes the living insult, my little man. And all the while, mind you, I was thinking to myself, while I was stubbing my silly toes against that cursed pyramid — so confoundedly contradictory was it all — all the while, I say, I was thinking to myself, 'What's his leg now but a cane — a whalebone cane? Yes,' thinks I, 'it was only a playful cudgeling — in fact, only a whaleboning he gave me — not a low kick. Besides,' thinks I, 'just look at it: why, the end of it — the foot part — what a small sort of end it is; whereas if a broad-footed farmer kicked me, now there's a devilish broad insult. But this insult is whittled down to a point.' But now comes the biggest joke of the dream, Flask. While I was battering away at the pyramid, a sort of badger-haired old merman with a hump on his back takes me by the shoulders and swings me round. 'What are you up to?' says he. Lord! man, but I was frightened. Such a mug! But somehow, the next moment I was over the fright. 'What am I up to?' says I at last. 'And what business is that of yours, I'd like to know, Mr. Humpback? Do you want a kick?' By the Lord, Flask, no sooner had I said that than he turned his stern to me, bent over, and, dragging up a lot of seaweed he wore for a loincloth — what do you think I saw? — why, thunder alive, man, his stern was stuck full of marlinspikes, with the points out. Says I, on second thought, 'I guess I won't kick you, old fellow.' 'Wise Stubb,' said he, 'wise Stubb,' and kept muttering it all the time, a sort of chewing on his own gums like an old hag by the chimney. Seeing he wasn't going to stop saying over his 'wise Stubb, wise Stubb,' I thought I might as well go back to kicking the pyramid. But I had only just lifted my foot for it when he roared out, 'Stop that kicking!' 'Hello,' says I, 'what's the matter now, old fellow?' 'Look here,' says he; 'let's argue the insult. Captain Ahab kicked you, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I — 'right here it was.' 'Very good,' says he — 'he used his ivory leg, didn't he?' 'Yes, he did,' says I. 'Well then,' says he, 'wise Stubb, what have you got to complain of? Didn't he kick with right good will? It wasn't a common pitch-pine leg he kicked with, was it? No, you were kicked by a great man, and with a beautiful ivory leg, Stubb. It's an honor; I consider it an honor. Listen, wise Stubb. In old England the greatest lords think it a great glory to be slapped by a queen and made Knights of the Garter; but let your boast be, Stubb, that you were kicked by old Ahab and made a wise man of. Remember what I say: be kicked by him; count his kicks as honors; and on no account kick back; for you can't help yourself, wise Stubb. Don't you see that pyramid?' With that, all of a sudden, he seemed somehow, in some queer fashion, to swim off into the air. I snored, rolled over, and there I was in my hammock! Now, what do you think of that dream, Flask?"
